b.bio: Martin Bouquet, born at Amiens on 6 August 1685 and died at the monastery of Blancs-Manteaux in Paris on 6 April 1754, was a Benedictine of the Congregation of St.-Maur. He took vows at St-Faron, Meaux, on 16 August 1706, served as librarian at St-Germain-des-Prés, assisted Montfaucon on Chrysostom, and passed his Josephus materials to Havercamp. His principal labor was editing Rerum Gallicarum et Francicarum Scriptores, a collection of historians of Gaul and France to 987, beginning with the first two volumes published in 1738. The three items held under his name are short 'Admonition' pieces printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volumes 97, 105, and 141.
b.s: A reader holding these works has not a treatise by Bouquet but his brief editorial admonitions preserved in Migne's reprinting of Maurist scholarship; his real monument is the Recueil des historiens des Gaules et de la France, which fixed the printed text of Merovingian and Carolingian sources.

b.bio: The library prints the name as Mariano Brockie; sources give Marianus Brockie. Born at Edinburgh on 2 December 1687, he joined the Scottish Benedictines at Ratisbon in 1708 and became doctor and professor of philosophy and divinity there, serving for a time as superior of the Scots monastery at Erfurt. From 1727 to 1739 he worked on the Catholic mission in Scotland, then returned to Ratisbon, where he was prior of St. James's for many years until his death on 2 December 1755. He compiled an unpublished Monasticon Scoticon (completed by Maurice Grant), later used by Gordon, and wrote critical-historical observations on monastic rules that were printed as volumes 3–6 of Holstenius's Codex Regularum (Augsburg, 1759) and reprinted by Migne in Patrologia Latina volumes 80, 87, and 88.
b.s: His Observationes critico-historicae are scholarly annotations on early monastic rules — including those attributed to Columbanus and to Donatus, bishop of Besançon — disputing attributions made by Calmet, Mabillon, and the compilers of the modern Scottish Monasticon.

b.bio: Surviving records do not clearly identify this author: they concern a twentieth-century Malankara Jacobite bishop named Mor Dionysius Michael, Dionysius Exiguus, and Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite — different persons entirely, to be ignored here. The library record shows that this Michael Dionysius wrote a prefatory address 'To the reader' printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina (vol. 46) concerning Augustine's sermons. In it he asserts that unpublished Augustinian sermons survive in the Viennese codex described by Lambecius, defends the genuineness of the anointing sermons, argues that Augustine repeats his own teachings deliberately, calls Augustine the most golden doctor of the church, and claims editors may correct manifest scribal errors while older manuscripts should confirm or overturn editorial conjectures.
b.s: His piece is a scholarly polemic over the authenticity of certain Augustinian sermons, opposing Bernard de Montfaucon, Jacob Sirmond, and the Maurist editors.

b.bio: Matthias Döring, born at Kyritz in Brandenburg between 1390 and 1400 and died there on 24 July 1469, was a German Franciscan who studied at Oxford and took his doctorate in theology at Erfurt in 1424. He taught theology and biblical exegesis, served as provincial of Saxony from 1427, and was prominent at the Council of Basle as a defender of conciliar supremacy over the pope. The Conventuals elected him minister general in 1443; he assisted in the deposition of Eugene IV and the election of antipope Felix V, was excommunicated by the Archbishop of Magdeburg, resigned in 1461, and spent his last years writing at Kyritz.
b.s: The library holds only the two-page prologue to his Replicae against Paul of Burgos's Additiones to Nicholas of Lyre's Postilla, where he defends literal exegesis of Scripture and argues that even unretracted sayings of Augustine remain opinable.

b.bio: Martin Gerbert, born at Horb am Neckar in Württemberg in August 1720, entered the Benedictine abbey of St. Blaise in the Black Forest, took vows there in 1737, was ordained priest in 1744, and taught philosophy and then theology while serving as librarian. Travels through Germany, Italy and France from about 1759 to 1762 to examine monastic archives turned him toward historical research; in 1760 he met Padre Martini at Bologna and shared his discoveries on music history; in 1764 he was elected prince-abbot of St. Blaise and made it a center of methodical historical study. His researches centered on liturgy and church music.
b.s: The works held here are his scholarly notices and admonitions on early music theorists — arguing that Hermann the Lame brought Guido of Arezzo to Bremen, that Guido rightly deserves the title inventor of music, and that Berno of Reichenau derived his theory from Guido — reflecting the archival research behind his history of church music.

b.bio: Marguerin de La Bigne was a French theologian and patrologist, born at Bernières-le-Patry, Normandy, around 1546. He studied at the College of Caen and at the Sorbonne in Paris, where he received the doctorate. He was named canon of his native Diocese of Bayeux and later dean of the church of Mans. At the Provincial Council of Rouen in 1581 he sustained the rights of his cathedral chapter against Bernadin de St. François, Bishop of Bayeux, provoking a conflict that ended with his resignation of the canonry. He then resumed patristic studies at the Sorbonne. Sources disagree on his death: the Catholic Encyclopedia gives about 1595, Wikipedia gives 1595 or 20 November 1597 at Paris, and Schaff-Herzog gives 1589.
b.s: He compiled and edited the Sacra Bibliotheca Sanctorum Patrum (Paris, 1575, 8 vols.), an anthology containing the writings of some two hundred Church Fathers, many published for the first time, undertaken to counter Protestant misquotation and misinterpretation of patristic texts; it is regarded as a pioneer work of critical patristics. The item held here is his Notice in PL 66.

w: On the exposition of the creed of Fortunatus

b.bio: Michelangelo Luchi (Luchius), born at Brescia on 20 August 1744, professed as a Benedictine at Monte Cassino, where he taught philosophy and theology. He searched Italian libraries for ancient manuscripts, many of which went to the Vatican. Pius VII made him a cardinal on 23 February 1801 and gave him charge of book censorship; he died at Subiaco on 29 September 1802. The other sources retrieved describe unrelated men named Michelangelo (the poet Torcigliani, the Protestant pastor Florio, Buonarroti); none of them is this author.
b.s: The pieces held here are his editorial prolegomena and dissertations for his edition of Venantius Fortunatus: he argues for Fortunatian authorship of the exposition of the creed and the life of Albinus (dating the latter after 576), dates the confessors' glory before 588, and disputes Surius, Valesius, Launoy, Muratori, Liruti and the authors of the Literary History of France.

b.bio: The library prints this name as Macarius of Nitria. The available biographical sources concern Macarius of Alexandria (called politicus or the Younger), a distinct figure from his contemporary Macarius of Egypt; because the identity of 'Macarius of Nitria' as printed cannot be confirmed against those sources, no biographical details (birth, trade, ordination, offices, death date) can be asserted here.
b.s: The two short works held here in PL 103 set out practical ascetic teaching: perfect charity requires loving God wholly; monastic obedience perfects the virtues of Christ; humility requires esteeming oneself inferior to all; obedience to the elder is received as salvation; good works must not occasion self-exaltation; the cell is the monk's paradise; the abbot is feared as master and loved as parent; nothing is to be preferred to prayer.

b.bio: The sources identify the Latinized name Maccabeus/Machabaeus with John Macalpine, a Scot born about the beginning of the sixteenth century who graduated at a Scottish university. He was prior of the Dominican convent of Perth from 1532 to 1534, then left for England after being summoned for heresy before the Bishop of Ross. He took a BA at Cologne, matriculated at Wittenberg in 1540, and received his doctorate there in 1542. That year Christian III of Denmark appointed him to the chair of theology at Copenhagen, where he helped build the Danish Lutheran church alongside Peter Plade and won Melanchthon's approval. He died at Copenhagen on 6 December 1557. A different figure, Saint Maccai (Maccæus), a fifth-century disciple of Patrick who founded a monastery on Bute, is a separate person and is not this author.
b.s: A Scottish Dominican turned Lutheran reformer whose theological work was done chiefly in Denmark; the single page held here treats true worship, the church, and the sacraments.

w: Booklet on the Mystery of Baptism

b.bio: The library's record identifies this author only by the name as printed and by two short Latin works on baptism and legal notes printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 102. No surviving record here gives dates, birthplace, or office for a Magnus of Sens, so none can be asserted. the surviving records describe different men: Odorannus of Sens (c. 985–1046), a Benedictine chronicler at Saint-Pierre-le-Vif, and Magnus Felix Ennodius (473/4–521), bishop of Pavia — neither matches these works, and both are set aside.
b.s: The booklet held here argues that baptism transforms man by the spirit of grace, that triple immersion signifies Christ's burial and resurrection, that it requires invocation of the Trinity, that infant faith is confessed by sponsors' hearts and mouths, and that original sin makes all slaves of the devil before baptism.

b.bio: Majolus (Maieul, Mayeul) was born around 906 at Avignon or Valensole to a wealthy family, studied at Lyons, and served as archdeacon of Mâcon before refusing election to the see of Besançon and entering Cluny as a monk about 942. Abbot Aymard made him apocrisiarius and librarian, then coadjutor in 954; he succeeded as abbot on Aymard's death in 965. He spread the Cluniac reform through Burgundy, Italy, and France, refused the papal tiara offered by Otto II in 974, and died at Souvigny in 994 while traveling to reform Saint-Denis for Hugh Capet.
b.s: The work held here is his account of the election of Odilo as abbot, a primary witness to how Cluny understood its authority — divine and papal foundations, obedience to Benedict's Rule, and election confirmed by counsel and subscription.

b.bio: The library prints this author simply as Mamertinus and holds one work under his name: an Act of Thanksgiving in PL 18. No surviving record describes this author — all four treat Claudianus Mamertus, the fifth-century Gallic monk and presbyter of Vienne who wrote De statu animae against Faustus of Riez, a different person with a similar name whose dates and biography cannot be transferred here. No source in hand confirms an identification with the late-Roman panegyrist of Emperor Julian, nor gives birth or death dates for this Mamertinus.
b.s: Per the library record, the held text is a formal speech of gratitude centering on the consulship as honor without labor, loyalty to the emperor against impious plots, and moral reform as harder than military victory; it argues against Constantius and his partisans, would-be tyrants such as Nepotianus and Silvanus, and Greek poets and rhetoricians. Its loci on the civil magistrate, providence, and virtue make it a document of imperial ideology rather than Christian theology.

b.bio: Manasses I de Gournay, son of Hugh II of Gournay-en-Bray, was a well-educated noble cleric before succeeding Gervase as Archbishop of Reims around 1069/1070, making him primate of France. Sources differ on the chronology of his fall: Wikipedia gives his deposition on 27 December 1080; the New Catholic Encyclopedia dates his election to 1070, his deposition to 1077, his excommunication by Gregory VII to 1080, and cannot trace him with certainty after May 1081, with death between 1081 and 1100. He defied the Gregorian reform and refused to answer charges of uncanonical conduct in council, and is remembered chiefly as patron of Fulcoius of Beauvais.
b.s: The library holds one letter addressed to the Morini under his name (PL 151); he matters less as an author than as the archbishop whose court at Reims was among the most intellectually vibrant in northern Europe before his fall.

b.bio: the surviving records describe three different men named Manfred or Manfredi: Fulgenzio Manfredi, a Franciscan preacher executed in Rome in 1610; the psychiatrist Manfred Lütz; and Manegold of Lautenbach, an eleventh-century polemicist. None matches the works held here, so none of these sources can be used for this author. The library's two items under the name 'Manfred' are Latin verse and prose on the calendar and creation, printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volumes 90 and 94: a short set of poems touching Creation, Christ as the true sun, the Trinity, and resurrection, and a one-page calculation of intercalary days defending the twenty-eight-year solar cycle, the nineteen- and twenty-four-year lunar circuits, the bissextus, and weekday names drawn from the seven planets.
b.s: These pieces belong to the early-medieval computistical tradition, joining cosmological exegesis to practical reckoning of leap days and epacts against holders of 'the previous error.'

b.bio: The library holds under the name Mangeantius a single two-page Admonition printed in PL 59. None of The surviving records concerns an author named Mangeantius; they cover Marius Mercator, Claudianus Mamertus, and Joannes Maxentius — different writers with different bodies of work — so they cannot be used to support any claim about this author. No dates, office, place, or biography can be asserted for Mangeantius from what is provided.
b.s: The Admonitio in PL 59 is the only work held here; its attribution and content rest on the library record alone.

b.bio: Mansuetus was Archbishop of Milan from 676 until his death, probably on 19 February 685. In 679 he held a synod at Milan with his suffragan bishops condemning Monothelitism, and a letter to Emperor Constantine IV setting out the faith was composed in his name by Damian, later bishop of Pavia. In 680 he attended and subscribed the Roman synod of Pope Agatho held in preparation for the Third Council of Constantinople. He is honoured as a saint; his feast is February 19 in the Roman Rite.
b.s: The work held here is his synodal epistle against Monothelitism, part of the Western conciliar action that preceded Constantinople III's condemnation of the doctrine of one will in Christ.

b.bio: Mantio (Mannon) was bishop of Châlons-sur-Marne (Catalaunensis), attested by a single letter dated 902 addressed to Fulk, archbishop of Reims. The letter concerns church discipline: it treats the correction and expulsion of married priests from the church, the suspension of an offending cleric pending judgment by a higher authority, and the principle that synods defer doctrinal and disciplinary judgment to the bishop. Nothing further about his life or episcopate is established in the sources at hand.
b.s: His one surviving letter is a witness to early tenth-century Gallican practice on clerical discipline and the hierarchical ordering of synodal judgment.

b.bio: Mappinius, bishop of Reims from 535 until 550, was a Gallic prelate of the Merovingian period; his name is of Gaulish origin. He did not attend the Fifth Council of Orléans in person, sending the archdeacon Protadius as his representative. Two letters survive, preserved in the Epistulae Austrasicae: one to Bishop Vilicus of Metz congratulating him on his seventieth birthday before asking about pig prices around Reims, and one to Bishop Nicetius of Trier excusing his absence from the Council of Toul in 550, which King Theudebald had convened concerning Nicetius' excommunication of Franks for incest.
b.s: The letters held here are among the few surviving sources for Merovingian episcopal politics, especially the dispute over excommunication and royal intervention at the Council of Toul.

b.bio: Marcellus Memorialis appears in Migne's Patrologia Latina, volume 11, as the author of a Praefatio and the Capitula gestorum (Chapters of Deeds), printed among the monuments concerning the Donatist schism in North Africa. The sources give no dates, office, or biography for him; he is known only through these two pieces. The works sit alongside Optatus of Milevis's De schismate Donatistarum and collections of imperial laws against the Donatists, indicating a writer concerned with the official record of proceedings in that controversy.
b.s: His Capitula gestorum and Preface preserve documentation of the acts against the Donatists, making his two short works part of the primary record of that schism.

b.bio: Marculf (printed here as Marculf of Paris) was a Frankish monk who wrote on customary law in the seventh century. Sources place his activity between 630 and 730; the Formulary is usually dated to the second half of the seventh century, sometimes c. 650. He was over seventy years old when he compiled it, and he dedicated it to a bishop named Landeric. The collection has two books: the first holds royal charters, the second private acts. It survives as the longest and best preserved formulary from the Merovingian kingdoms, with a preface and a coherent manuscript transmission.
b.s: The work held here is not doctrinal theology but a legal handbook: model documents for royal grants, confirmations of ecclesiastical property, and private transactions, showing how kings, bishops, and churches handled law and land in Merovingian Gaul.

b.bio: The library holds one work under this name: a poem on Saint Benedict printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 80. The devotional sources retrieved describe a 'Marcius' or 'Marcus' as a Benedictine hermit of Monte Cassino, said to have lived in a cave on Mount Mondragone and to be mentioned by Pope Gregory the Great; they give no dates and attribute no writings to him. That hermit cannot be confirmed as the poet who wrote the work held here, and the two may be distinct persons sharing a name. Nothing else about the author's life, dates, or office is established here.
b.s: His poem presents Benedict as the saint who overturns pagan worship—profaning idols as works of human hands, converting temples of Jove, making barren hearts fruitful—and whose intercession obtains salvation for others.

b.bio: Marcus of Otranto (Hydruntis) is placed in the eighth century; Allatius reports that before becoming bishop he served as oeconomus, or steward, of the great church of Constantinople, and this is nearly all that is recorded of him. He wrote an acrostic hymn for Holy Saturday (In Magnum Sabbatum), whose opening letters spell the Greek phrase 'kai semeron de'. It was printed by Aldus Manutius with a Latin version in his edition of Prudentius and other early Christian poets (Venice, c. 1501), and appears in Migne's Patrologia Latina 96. The library holds this single-page Latin hymn.
b.s: The work here is a Holy Saturday hymn on Christ's descent: his death destroys death and opens hell, he preaches to the souls there, renews Adam's corrupted race, reunites divided humanity through his outstretched arms on the cross, and by assuming flesh deifies it and makes it incorruptible — a liturgical witness to the harrowing-of-hades theology shared between Greek East and Latin West.

b.bio: Marcus Minucius Felix was a Roman legal practitioner and one of the earliest Christian apologists to write in Latin. Jerome calls him 'Romae insignis causidicus,' a courtroom advocate. His personal history is otherwise unknown; the date of his writing can only be placed approximately between AD 150 and 270, and Britannica gives his death as c. 250 in Rome, with a possible African origin. He was a convert to Christianity. His single known work, the Octavius, stages a dialogue between the pagan skeptic Caecilius Natalis and the Christian Octavius Januarius, borrowing its arguments chiefly from Cicero's De natura deorum and from the Greek apologists.
b.s: The Octavius held here is among the earliest Latin apologetic works: a Ciceronian dialogue defending providence and Christianity against pagan skepticism, written for educated non-Christians.

b.bio: Marianus Scotus (Máel Brigte, 'Brigit's servant') was an Irish monk born in 1028. He became a monk in 1052 and left Ireland in 1056 after being expelled by his abbot Tigernach Bairrchech, passing through St Martin's at Cologne and Fulda before being enclosed as a recluse. Ordained priest at Würzburg in 1059, he was transferred in 1069/70 by Siegfried, bishop of Mainz, to St Martin's there, where he died on 22 December 1082 or 1083. His world chronicle, written under a dual dating scheme that held Dionysius Exiguus had erred by 22 years, circulated widely and was used in England by John of Worcester and Florence of Worcester.
b.s: The work held here is his universal Chronicle, a year-by-year history from creation to 1082 whose chronological revision of the Christian era and its accounts of councils, emperors, and heresiarchs made it a standard medieval source.

b.bio: Marius of Avenches was born near Autun around 530 to a distinguished, probably Gallo-Roman family and became Bishop of Aventicum (Avenches) in 574. He attended the Council of Mâcon in 585 and shortly afterwards moved his see from the declining Avenches to Lausanne, where he died — sources disagree on the year, giving either 31 December 594 or 596. Venerated as a saint in Lausanne, he is remembered almost solely for a terse chronicle continuing Prosper of Aquitaine.
b.s: His Chronicle (455–581), a continuation of Prosper of Aquitaine, uniquely transmits Burgundian affairs after 533/534 and reports contemporary events in Italy and the East; the library holds this chronicle in Migne's PL 72.

b.bio: A monk named Martinianus whose only surviving work here is a two-page Prologue to the Moral Books, printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina vol. 131. Nothing in the available evidence dates him or locates his monastery; the prologue itself is all that identifies him.
b.s: His prologue frames temptation and the inward struggle: the devil tempts believers as he tempted Adam, God alone sees the hidden struggle, and deliverance comes by grace through Christ, who undoes the death brought by the forbidden tree.

b.bio: Born in Pannonia about 520, Martin became a monk in the Holy Land and came to Gallaecia around 550 to convert the Suevi, some still pagan or Arian. He founded monasteries, including Dumio, where he was abbot and then bishop, signing the Synod of Braga of 561 as Bishop of Dumio. He later became Archbishop of Braga and presided over the second Council of Braga in 572. Gregory of Tours called him second to none of his contemporaries in learning. He died at Braga in 580; his feast is 20 March.
b.s: The works held here are his moral and ascetical treatises — on anger, pride, humility, honest living — which provided an influential model for the religious instruction that shaped the later conversion of northern and eastern Europe.

b.bio: Martin was born at Sabaria in Pannonia to pagan parents and raised partly at Pavia; he served in the Roman army in Gaul before leaving military service, becoming a disciple of Hilary of Poitiers and founding a monastery at Ligugé around 360. He was consecrated bishop of Tours in 371 and held the see until his death at Candes on 8 November 397. Sulpicius Severus, his contemporary, wrote his Life. Sources differ on his birth year (316 or 336), so the range here is wide.
b.s: The library holds one work under this name, a Confession asserting the unity of essence among the three divine persons and the incomprehensibility of God — doctrine consistent with fourth-century anti-Arian theology, though readers should note that this text's attribution within Migne's Patrologia Latina vol. 18 should be weighed against the better-attested picture of Martin as monk-bishop rather than author.

w: Epistle of Matilda and Critical-Historical-Exegetical Commentary

b.bio:
Matilda, Queen of the Franks (c. 892 – 14 March 968) — Several medieval women named Matilda appear in the sources: Matilda of Frisia (d. 1044), queen of the Franks as first wife of Henry I of France; Matilda of Flanders (d. 1083), queen of England; and Matilda of Ringelheim (c. 892 – 14 March 968), wife of Henry the Fowler and mother of Otto the Great. The library prints the name as 'Queen of the Franks,' but the single work held under this name cites Thietmar, Widukind, Otto the Great, and Otto III, and concerns a manuscript of the Roman liturgy donated by a Mathilda to Micy — an Ottonian-Saxon frame pointing to Matilda of Ringelheim rather than the French queens. She was born around 892 (one source says about 895) at Enger/Engern in Saxony/Westphalia, raised at Herford Abbey, married Henry in 909, founded several spiritual institutions and women's convents, and died at Quedlinburg on 14 March 968.

Philippe-Antoine Detherius (1803–1881) — Philipp Anton Dethier (printed here as Philippe-Antoine Detherius) is documented in Deutsche Biographie with life dates 1803–1881 and Latinized name forms including Dethierus, Philippus A.; the entry gives no further biographical detail beyond these names and dates, so his profession as historian or archivist is inferred from the character of the work held here rather than independently attested. The other surviving records describe different men: Cardinal Philippe-Antoine Gualterio (1660–1728), Philip the Chancellor of Paris (d. 1236), and Philippe-André Grandidier (1752–1787); none of these is this author. The work held under his name is a critical-historical-exegetical commentary on an eleventh-century epistle of Matilda concerning a manuscript of the Roman liturgy donated to Mieszko (Misego).
b.s: The single work held here is not by her but a critical-historical-exegetical commentary on an epistle transmitted under her name, arguing from contemporary German sources (Thietmar, Widukind) against Roepell, Raczynski, Długosz, and Polish historians of the Roman rite that the manuscript is an eleventh-century Roman liturgy (dated by mixed letter forms), that Charlemagne and Alcuin composed the pseudo-Alcuin liturgy, and that early medieval sources are scarce enough to require conjecture.

b.bio: Matthew of Albano was born in the country of Laon, France, perhaps around 1085, studied under Anselm there, and entered the Cluniac priory of Saint-Martin-des-Champs in Paris in 1110, becoming its prior seven years later. Pope Honorius II created him cardinal bishop of Albano in 1125, and Innocent II sent him as legate to France (1127) and Germany (1128) to restore monastic discipline. He helped secure recognition for the Knights Templar at the Council of Troyes in 1129, defended Abbot Peter the Venerable against the deposed Abbot Pons before Honorius II, and after the Council of Pisa (1134) was invited by Bernard of Clairvaux to restore Milan to papal obedience. He died at Pisa on December 25, 1135.
b.s: The letters and diplomas held here show him as legate ruling that canons may present priests without simony, that the bishop alone commits care of souls to priests and holds coercive jurisdiction, that abbots are freely elected by monastic chapters under anathema against violation of electoral liberty, and that papal authority saves local concords — documents of twelfth-century church governance issued under papal authority.

b.bio: Maurice de Sully, born of humble parents at Sully-sur-Loire near Orléans at the beginning of the twelfth century, came to Paris around 1140, became a professor of theology and preacher, appears as Archdeacon of Paris in 1159, and on 12 October 1160 was elected Bishop of Paris, succeeding Peter Lombard, largely through Louis VII's influence. He held the see until his retirement in 1196 and died at Paris on 11 September 1196. His episcopate saw the construction of Notre-Dame cathedral: Alexander III laid its cornerstone in 1163. The library holds only five pages of letters and diplomas under his name (PL 205) — charters concerning a census rightfully held by Saint-Victor by gift, a quitclaim by Ferricus de Gentiliaco of that census to Saint-Victor forever, ordinances expanding divine worship deserving perpetual confirmation, the full parochial rights of a baptismal church, and a patron's right of presentation with episcopal rights reserved.
b.s: The builder-bishop of Notre-Dame; the works here are administrative charters showing episcopal governance of parochial rights and monastic endowments rather than theology.

b.bio: Maurilius was born around 1000 near Reims, studied at Liège, taught at Halberstadt, became a monk at Fécamp, lived as a hermit in Italy, and served briefly as abbot of St Mary's in Florence before returning to Fécamp. After the deposition of Mauger at Lisieux (1054 or 1055), Duke William appointed him Archbishop of Rouen. He promoted church reform, presided over a provincial council at Caen imposing the Truce of God under pain of excommunication, saw the work on Rouen Cathedral completed and dedicated (1063), and moved the bodies of Dukes Rollo and William into it. He died in 1067.
b.s: The works held here are his epitaph for Rollo and William Longsword, a profession of faith, and a letter to the Bishop of Évreux asserting that the Benedictine rule stands above secular legal judgment and that a bishop has no right in a monastery without the abbot's invitation.

w: Letter to the Bishop of Évreux

b.bio:
Maurilius of Rouen (c. 1000–1067) — Maurilius was born around 1000 near Reims, studied at Liège, taught at Halberstadt, became a monk at Fécamp, lived as a hermit in Italy, and served briefly as abbot of St Mary's in Florence before returning to Fécamp. After the deposition of Mauger at Lisieux (1054 or 1055), Duke William appointed him Archbishop of Rouen. He promoted church reform, presided over a provincial council at Caen imposing the Truce of God under pain of excommunication, saw the work on Rouen Cathedral completed and dedicated (1063), and moved the bodies of Dukes Rollo and William into it. He died in 1067.

John of Fécamp (d. 1079) — Born near Ravenna in the early eleventh century, John followed his uncle William of Volpiano to the abbey of Saint-Bénigne at Dijon, then to Fécamp, where he served as prior until 1028 and succeeded William as abbot. In 1052 he was invited to Dijon as abbot, holding both houses until he resigned Fécamp in 1056. He died at Fécamp on 22 February 1079. He wrote under the names of famous authors, notably the Meditations attributed to St. Augustine, which circulated widely before the Imitation of Christ displaced them. The library's record also shows attribution questions around his prayer book: a Metz codex of about 1080, prayers secondarily assigned to Anselm, and a prayer attributed to William of Metz.
b.s: The works held here are his epitaph for Rollo and William Longsword, a profession of faith, and a letter to the Bishop of Évreux asserting that the Benedictine rule stands above secular legal judgment and that a bishop has no right in a monastery without the abbot's invitation.

w: Index of letters according to their subjects
Inquiry into the Writings of Gerbert

b.bio: The Maurist Editors were the scholarly Benedictine monks of the French Congregation of Saint Maur who, during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, revolutionized the critical study of Christian antiquity. Based primarily at the Abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés in Paris, these scholars—including figures such as Jean Mabillon and Bernard de Montfaucon—pioneered modern historical-critical methods and textual criticism. They prepared monumental editions of the Latin and Greek Church Fathers, supplying each treatise with rigorous manuscript collations and introductory critical prefaces titled 'Admonitiones'. Their editions formed the authoritative foundation for later major patristic compilations, most notably J.-P. Migne's Patrologia Latina.
b.s: The Maurist Editors established modern textual criticism in patristics, producing landmark editions of the Church Fathers that remained the scholarly standard for centuries.

b.bio: Mauros (Maurus) was bishop of Ravenna in 649. Invited by Pope Martin I to the Lateran Council of October 649, he replied that barbarian incursions and the absence of an escort prevented him from attending in person; the bishop of Caesena and a Ravennate priest represented him at all five sessions. The Liber Pontificalis records that under Pope Donus (676–678) the schism Maurus had begun — an attempt to make Ravenna ecclesiastically independent of Rome — was ended when Donus received the obedience of Maurus' successor Reparatus. The epistle held here is his anti-monothelite letter against Pyrrhus, former patriarch of Constantinople.
b.s: His single surviving epistle is a contemporary Latin witness to the two-wills, two-operations Christology affirmed at the Lateran Council of 649 and later at Constantinople III.

w: Collectanea on the ancient rites of baptism

b.bio: Maxentius was patriarch of Aquileia from 811, succeeding Ursus, and petitioned Charlemagne's court for funds to rebuild the city. His patriarchate was marked by a long jurisdictional dispute with Venerius of Grado over Istrian bishoprics, settled in Aquileia's favor at the Synod of Mantua in June 827. Sources differ on his death date: one gives 837, another 833/8. Some texts transmitted under his name are attributed to a Pseudo-Maxentius.
b.s: The works held here — a Collectanea on ancient baptismal rites and a letter to Charlemagne — preserve an early ninth-century account of the catechumenate: exorcism, salt, and sponsors' renunciations on behalf of infants, framed by the apostles' symbol as a common preaching norm.

b.bio:
Maximus Africanus (unknown) — The library holds one short epistle under the printed name 'Maximus Africanus' in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 3. No source consulted describes an author by this exact name; they describe two different men with whom the printed name could be conflated — Maximus of Turin (c. 380 – shortly after 465), first known bishop of Turin and a theological writer and preacher who helped consolidate Christianity in northern Italy, and Sextus Julius Africanus (c. 160–c. 240), a Greek-writing Christian historian and 'father of Christian chronography' whose Chronicle influenced Eusebius and later chroniclers. Which, if either, stands behind the epistle held here cannot be established from these sources.

Urbanus (unknown) — The library holds one short epistle under the name Urbanus in PL 3. The name is associated with the Ante-Nicene fragments printed under 'Asterius Urbanus', a writer whose extant fragments are dated to the latter part of the second century and who is associated with Eusebius of Caesarea. CCEL describes him as a follower of Montanus whose extant fragments nonetheless argue against some of Montanus' teachings, so he is labeled both a Montanist and an anti-Montanist author. He should not be confused with Urban I, bishop of Rome (c. 222/223–230), or the New Testament Urbanus of Romans 16:9.

Sidonius (c. c. 430–490) — Gaius Sollius Modestus Apollinaris Sidonius, born at Lyons on 5 November about 430, came from a Gallo-Roman aristocratic family; his father and grandfather had been prefects of the praetorium of the Gauls. He married Papianilla, daughter of the emperor Avitus, wrote panegyrics on Avitus, Majorian, and Anthemius, and served as Urban prefect of Rome under Anthemius in 468. Elected bishop of the Arverni (Clermont) around 469–470 against his wishes, he led the city's defence against Euric's Visigoths from 473 to 475 and held the see until his death in the early 480s. About 147 letters and 24 poems survive.

Macharius (unknown) — Macharius is the name under which this library holds a single short epistle printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 3, the volume devoted to the works attributed to Dionysius the Areopagite. No source identifies an author behind the name: no dates, office, or biography are attested for him here. A separate medieval tradition (a Passio of Denis) gives 'Macharius' as the Christian baptismal name of Dionysius the Areopagite himself, and other writers named Macarius — Macarius Magnes, a Christian apologist of the late fourth century, probably identical with the bishop of Magnesia who acted at the Synod of the Oak in 403 and author of the Apocritica, or the pseudo-Macarius whose Regula monachorum is preserved in medieval manuscripts — are different figures whose works do not match what is held here.
b.s: The work held here is a single-page epistle in PL 3; its attribution to either Maximus of Turin or Julius Africanus is not settled by the sources consulted.

b.bio: Maximus was bishop of Zaragoza from 592 until his death around 619, the first Visigothic-era holder of that see. He held the Second Council of Zaragoza against Arianism in 592 and signed the acts of councils at Barcelona (599), Toledo (610), and Egara (614). Isidore of Seville praises him as one of three sixth-century chroniclers and notes he wrote other works in prose and verse. The Chronicle printed under his name in PL 80 was edited by Higuera in 1611 and is regarded as a forgery; only 33 brief anonymous excerpts survive of any genuine chronicle.
b.s: The works here are an epistle and a chronicle from PL 80; the chronicle is a seventeenth-century forgery, so readers should treat the volume as evidence of early modern editorial fabrication rather than of Maximus's own hand. The surviving pages treat Chalcedon's confirmation of Leo's doctrine of the incarnation and the Vandal persecution of Catholics.

b.bio: Maximus of Madaura was a pagan grammarian in the North African town of Madaura, active around 390. He corresponded with Augustine of Hippo: his letter (Augustine, Letter 16) defends traditional Roman religion against Christian claims, objecting that African martyrs such as Miggin, Sanam, Namphamon and Lucitas receive more veneration than the pagan gods, while affirming a single supreme God whose powers are worshipped under many names. Augustine's reply is preserved as Letter 17.
b.s: His surviving exchange with Augustine is one of the clearest records of an educated pagan challenging Christianity in provincial North Africa after its official adoption, conducted with mutual respect rather than polemic.

w: On the Life and Virtues of Emmeram

b.bio: Meginfred of Magdeburg is attested in the first half of the eleventh century as scholasticus (Domscholaster) at Magdeburg, and in some records as provost (praepositus). He is named only in the dedicatory letter to Arnold of St. Emmeram's Miracula sancti Emmerammi; beyond that the sources record nothing of his life. The library holds his Vita sancti Emmerammi (BHL 2540), an account of the martyr-bishop Emmeram of Regensburg that treats his virtues and miracles and defends the veneration owed to martyrs who intercede for the faithful.
b.s: His surviving work is a hagiographical vita of Emmeram of Regensburg arguing for the merits, intercession, and cult of the martyr.

b.bio: Melchior a Vosmediano is Melchor Alvarez de Vozmediano, born at Carrión de los Condes in the diocese of Palencia and bishop (later Bishop Emeritus) of Guadix in Spain. He died on 24 November 1587. In 1565 he served as principal co-consecrator of Bishop Pedro de la Peña, O.P. The two pages held here under his name are preliminary matter: a dedication letter and an address to the reader printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 161.
b.s: He appears in this library only as the voice of the dedicatory letter and address to the reader prefacing texts in PL 161; the substantive content of those texts belongs to other authors.

b.bio: Mengoz was a canon of the early twelfth century known from a single letter addressed to Rupert of Deutz, abbot of Deutz (dated 1120–1129 in the source). The letter defends the author against disparagers, arguing that disputes about creatures do not endanger faith: God alone is the salvation and life of creatures, and error about God is dangerous while error about creatures is not. It treats angels, God, and Scripture, and cites 'the father of lights' and the author of On the Victory of the Word of God. Nothing further about his life is recorded here.
b.s: The library holds only this one-page epistle, a short polemic distinguishing errors about God from errors about creatures, preserved among Rupert of Deutz's correspondence in PL 170.

b.bio: Flavius Merobaudes was a fifth-century Latin rhetorician and poet, probably a native of Baetica in Spain, of Frankish origin. He served as official laureate to Valentinian III and Aetius, campaigned with Aetius in the Alps, and was honored with statues at Rome (inscription of 435, CIL VI 1724). Until Niebuhr's discovery of verses on a St Gall palimpsest (published 1824), he was known only from Hydatius' Chronicle (year 443). The short poem De Christo (30 hexameters) is attributed to him by one manuscript and to Claudian by another; Ebert disputed both his authorship and his Christianity, while Birt upheld the attribution.
b.s: The library holds only the De Christo, a brief hymn whose attribution is contested; it matters chiefly as evidence for how Christian Latin poets adapted Virgilian diction such as 'repertor' for Christ as creator.

b.bio:
Michael Keroularios (c. c. 1000–1059) — Michael Keroularios was Patriarch of Constantinople from 1043 until his deposition on 2 November 1058; he died on 21 January 1059. Born in Constantinople around 1000 to a leading family, he first pursued a court career, plotted with Constantine Monomachus against Emperor Michael IV, and entered a monastery after his brother's suicide. As patriarch he quarrelled with Pope Leo IX over the use of unleavened bread in the Eucharist and over papal supremacy and the Filioque, exchanges that fed into the schism of 1054. The letter held here defends leavened eucharistic bread and answers Latin practice.

Leo of Ohrid (d. 1056) — Leo of Ohrid was Archbishop of Ohrid from 1037 until his death in 1056, having earlier served as chartophylax at Hagia Sophia in Constantinople. Under Patriarch Michael Keroularios he acted as Constantinople's spokesman in disputes with Latin clergy in southern Italy. His 1053 letter to John of Trani — addressed to the Pope and all Latin bishops — attacked Western liturgical and disciplinary practices and set off the exchanges that ended in his excommunication by Cardinal Humbert's legation in 1054.
b.s: His dispute with Rome made him a central figure in the Great Schism of 1054, and the letter here is part of that controversy: it argues for leavened bread as life-giving and paschal, against unleavened Latin usage and Judaizing readings of the rite.

b.bio: Milo Crispin was a monk and cantor of the Benedictine Abbey of Bec, of the noble Crispin family descended from the Neustrian Gislebert; his brother Gilbert, later Abbot of Westminster, wrote the life of Herluin, Bec's founder. Milo wrote lives of five abbots of Bec: Lanfranc, William of Bellême (Gulielmus de Bellomonte), Boso, Theobaldus, and Letardus. The life of Lanfranc is printed in the Acta Sanctorum (May 28); the other four are in PL 150, those of Theobaldus and Letardus being mere summaries. In the last chapter of his life of Lanfranc he reports something he himself heard Anselm say; since Anselm died in 1109 and Letardus not until 1149, his religious life spanned more than forty years. No details of his career are preserved.
b.s: His Life of Blessed Lanfranc and Life of William of Bec are the principal narrative sources for Lanfranc's career at Bec and Canterbury, including his teaching against Berengar and Roscelin and his death on 28 May 1089.

b.bio: A French Benedictine of the abbey of Saint-Aubin at Angers, born early in the 11th century. His abbot sent him to Rome to Pope Urban II, who made him a cardinal and bishop of Palestine; he was later sent back to France to preach against simony. He attended the Council of Clermont in 1095 and served as papal legate under Paschal II after Urban's death. Marbode wrote a eulogy for him, published by Mabillon. Martène printed verses by a certain Milon believed to be this bishop's.
b.s: The library holds metrical verse from PL 163 — Latin poetry citing classical authors (Aristotle, Cicero/Tully, Plato, Ovid/Naso) — which Martène attributed (with some uncertainty) to the bishop of Palestine.

b.bio: Marcellinus Molkenbuhr (baptismal name Bernd Anton) was born on 1 September 1741 in Rheine in Westphalia and entered the Franciscan province of Saxonia at Hamm in 1758. After studies at his order's houses in Warendorf (philosophy), Halberstadt (dogmatic and moral theology) and Bielefeld (exegesis and canon law) he was ordained priest in October 1764. He taught philosophy at Geseke, Vreden and Rietberg from 1766 to 1774, then dogmatic and moral theology at Paderborn from 1774 to 1786. He later served as Guardian of Paderborn, three times Provincial of Saxonia (1789–92, 1798–1801, 1807–10), Custos (1787 and 1805), provincial secretary, and visitator generalis (1804). He died at Paderborn on 16 June 1825.
b.s: His dissertations here are critical-historical defenses: one argues that Pope Honorius was never condemned for heresy and that neither Honorius nor the council erred over the Ecthesis, the other defends the authenticity of Firmilian's letter to Stephen and fixes the date of the synod against Paul of Samosata.

w: Encyclical Letter on the Murder of Abbo

b.bio: This name covers the community of monks at Fleury Abbey in the time of Abbot Abbo, who was killed on 13 November 1004 during a dispute at the monastery of La Réole in Gascony. A single-page encyclical letter on Abbo's murder is preserved under this collective authorship in Migne's Patrologia Latina, volume 139. The surviving records describe individual Fleury authors — Abbo himself, Aimoin, Hugh of Fleury — and do not document this collective authorship or the circumstances of the letter's issuance, so no further biographical detail can be asserted for the monks as a body.
b.s: The single work held here is an announcement of Abbo's death, framing death suffered for religion as meriting fellowship with martyrs and commending the prayers of saints for departed souls.

w: Appendix to the History of the Kings of the Franks

b.bio: An anonymous author or authors writing under the abbey's name ('Monks of Saint-Denis' as printed). The library holds a thirteen-page appendix to a history of the kings of the Franks printed in PL 163. Its content is political-ecclesiastical narrative: it asserts that the Roman see is head of all churches, that pious kings endow churches with lands and that such endowments are irrevocable under oath, and it condemns usurpers against rightful heirs. It names Hugh Capet and his council, Grimoald mayor of the Austrasian palace, and clerics led by Frotmund as opponents, and treats the Constantinopolitan church and the Hebrews as foils to Frankish orthodoxy.
b.s: The appendix is a Saint-Denis legitimist text defending rightful royal succession and the irrevocability of church endowments against Hugh Capet's accession and other usurpations.

b.bio: This entry covers works attributed collectively to the monks of La Sauve-Majeure (Grande-Sauve), the abbey founded in 1079 in the forest of Silva Major east of Bordeaux by Gerald of Corbie (c. 1025–1095) with land granted by Duke William VIII of Aquitaine, free of lay feudal control and directly subject to the Holy See. The library holds one work under this corporate name: Commemorations, printed in PL 147, which treats prayer in historical form. No source gives dates or offices for the community as an author; the biographical material in the sources concerns its founder, not the monks as such.
b.s: The work held here is a historical treatment of prayer from a reformed eleventh-century Aquitanian abbey, preserved in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 147.

w: Letter on the Death of Abbot Bernard

b.bio: The library's single work under this name is a two-page letter on the death of an Abbot Bernard, printed in PL 155. The letter records that Anselm died in the year 1100, which places its authors in the early twelfth century or later. the surviving records describe other bearers of the Tours name — Gregory of Tours, the sixth-century bishop and historian, and Martin of Tours, the fourth-century bishop — neither of whom matches a work citing Anselm's death; they are different persons and are disregarded.
b.s: The letter is a short monastic consolatio treating the church as Christ's body whose members suffer together, affirming postmortem purgation of venial stains and the efficacy of the living's prayers for souls in purgatory.

w: Admonition on the Gift of Perseverance

b.bio: This entry stands for a collective attribution rather than a single identifiable writer. None of the named Benedictines covered by the surviving records here—Jean Mabillon, Prosper Guéranger, Lucas d'Achery, or Guibert of Nogent—can be attached to the work held under this name, and no source gives dates or a particular monastery for its author. The 'Admonition on the Gift of Perseverance' printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 45 is held by the library under this collective attribution; readers should treat the Benedictine attribution with caution and consult the work itself for its teaching.
b.s: The library holds one work under this name, an admonition on perseverance as a gift of grace, catalogued in PL 45.

b.bio: An anonymous Bohemian monastic author, printed under a name easily confused with the Norman abbey of Savigny but identifiable by his subject matter: he continues the chronicle of Cosmas of Prague into the reign of Duke Soběslav I. His pages concern an abbacy in Bohemia contested between the community's lawful election of an abbot and a Teutonic abbot installed by the duke, with Abbot Božetech among the opponents named. He defends Slavonic letters as canonically established by Cyril, which points to the milieu of the Sázava monastery with its Old Church Slavonic tradition. the surviving records for this note describe Vitalis of Savigny and Godfrey of Savigny, twelfth-century Normans; they are different men and are not used here.
b.s: His continuation of Cosmas is a primary narrative for early-twelfth-century Bohemia and a polemic for canonical abbatial election and the Slavonic liturgy against ducal interference.

b.bio: Montanus succeeded Celsus in the see of Toledo, the prima sedes of the province of Carthaginensis. Ildefonsus' brief life of him records that he defended his office, wrote two letters on church discipline—one to the inhabitants of Palencia, one to Turibius—and rebutted a scandalous accusation by a miracle. He presided over the second council of Toledo, which opened on May 17 in the fifth year of Amalaric (a.d. 527 by the reckoning generally adopted since Florez, 531 by the older reckoning); the Acts have been suspected of interpolation but are generally accepted as genuine. McClintock and Strong instead place his succession in 531 and death in 540. The two letters held here (PL 65) correspond to those Ildefonsus mentions.
b.s: His surviving letters are early witnesses to Visigothic-era Spanish discipline: they insist that no one may exercise sacred offices without holding them, reserve chrism and church consecration to bishops, treat usurpation of sacramental rites as schism, and attack Priscillianist remnants and presuming priests in his province.

b.bio: Born at Cividale del Friuli in 1536 to a family of Venetian origin, Nicoletti served as notary and chancellor of the commune and of the monastery of Santa Maria in Valle. From the city archives he gathered extensive material on Friulian and Cividalese affairs under the patriarchs. He died in 1596, accidentally shot during factional clashes in the city. His manuscripts passed to Francesco di Manzano, who drew on them for his own histories.
b.s: The work held here is his Second Life of St. Paulinus, a historical compilation built from the chapter cartulary of Friuli and Paul the Deacon, defending image veneration against the iconoclasts and opposing Elipandus and Felix of Urgel.

b.bio: Michael Pleunich was a printer active in Venice in the mid-eighteenth century. The library record under his name holds not a theological work by him but the imprint he produced: the 'Editio veneta novissima' of the collected works of Rupert, abbot of Deutz, printed in Venice in four folio volumes between 1748 and 1751, with frontispiece. The note accompanying it presents this new edition as making Rupert's works affordable and credits its patrons with meriting honor from the republic of letters. No surviving record gives dates or further biographical details for Pleunich himself.
b.s: He matters here as the printer of the 1748–1751 Venetian edition of Rupert of Deutz's Opera, the text tradition through which many readers encountered that twelfth-century abbot's works.

b.t: Roman grammarian and critic (1st century AD)
b.bio: Marcus Valerius Probus, sometimes called Berytius or Probus the Berytian, was a Roman grammarian and critic from Berytus who flourished during Nero's reign. Having served in the army and applied unsuccessfully for promotion, he turned in disgust to literary pursuits. He was a student rather than a teacher, devoting himself to the criticism and elucidation of the texts of classical authors — especially Horace, Lucretius, Terence and Persius (and, according to some accounts, Virgil) — by marginal notes or signs, after the manner of the Alexandrine grammarians. With the exception of these texts he published little; his lectures were preserved in notes taken by his pupils.
b.s: The library holds a short minor work on ancient notes (9 pages), which cites Bede; it is not identified with the surviving fragment of Probus's treatise De notis, so no claim about De notis being held here can be made from the record alone.

b.bio: English classical and patristic scholar, born at South Elmham, Suffolk. Educated at Queen's College, Oxford (matriculated 1770), then a demy and fellow of Magdalen College; college librarian from 1781, and President of Magdalen from 1791 until his death sixty-three years later. Ordained deacon in 1777 but not priested until 1810, when he became rector of Tylehurst near Reading. His chief work was the Reliquiae Sacrae (1814–18; 2nd ed. 1846–48), a collection of patristic fragments with critical commentary.
b.s: The annotations held here are textual-critical notes on Cyprian, arguing that Manutius's conjectural emendations lack manuscript authority and defending older edition readings against Baluze, Fell, and Pamelius.

b.bio: Synodus Mesopotamica is the name under which the library holds a single page from Migne's Patrologia Latina (vol. 5): the Actio of a 'divine and sacred particular synod' collected in Mesopotamia by Archelaus, bishop of Carchar, and Diodorus, a priest, against Mani and the presbyter Diodoriades. The Documenta Catholica Omnia record dates the document to 282. It is not the work of an individual author but a conciliar act transmitted in Latin.
b.s: The Actio records a synodal condemnation of Mani and his follower Diodoriades, 'refuted in many ways and cast out,' making it one of the earliest anti-Manichaean documents.

b.bio: Matthias Agricius (born Bauer at Wittlich; Latinized as Witlichius) was a Catholic humanist poet and historian of the Trier region. Sources record his birth in 1545 at Wittlich and death in 1613 at Himmerod near Wittlich. His published works are Latin verse: elegiac and heroic poems on saints' lives, an encomium of dawn, a book of prayers gathered from Scripture and the fathers, and the Fasti Trevirenses (1587), which versifies sixty-one saintly lives and describes the exposition of the Holy Robe at Trier in 1585. The library holds under his name a four-page declamation defending Rupert of Deutz against his slanderers.
b.s: The work held here is a four-page polemic defending Rupert of Deutz's eloquence and monastic learning against detractors, arguing that virtue rather than birth makes the man and that piety satisfies the soul.

b.bio: Magnoald Ziegelbauer was a Benedictine monk born at Ellwangen in Swabia. He took vows at Zwiefalten on 21 November 1707, was ordained priest on 21 March 1713, and became professor of theology there before moving to Reichenau, where he also taught theology, and later to Göttweig (moral theology, 1732–33) and Vienna for literary work. From 1747 he served as secretary of the Societas incognitorum at Olmütz, where he died on 14 January 1750. His chief work is the Historia rei literariae ordinis S. Benedicti, published posthumously by Oliver Legipontius (4 vols., Augsburg, 1754). The library holds only a two-page historical notice from him under PL 141.
b.s: He matters as the author of the standard literary history of the Benedictine Order; the item held here is a brief historical notice printed among Migne's Patrologia Latina volumes.

w: Melito, Bishop of Sardis in Asia: Notices and Fragments

b.bio: Melito was bishop of Sardis in Lydia in the latter half of the second century and held a foremost place among the early Christian bishops of Roman Asia due to his personal influence and literary works. Polycrates of Ephesus, writing to Pope Victor about 194 (Eusebius, Church History V.24), calls him a eunuch (rendered 'virgin' by Rufinus) whose whole walk was in the Holy Spirit and names him among the great authorities of the Asian church that kept the Quartodeciman Easter observance. Eusebius gives the titles of twenty of his Greek books; nearly all are lost except fragments and his homily on the Passion. He wrote an Apology to Marcus Aurelius appealing to him to examine the accusations against Christians and to end persecution, drew up an early Old Testament canon list, and is cited in Hippolytus' Labyrinth as teaching the duality of natures in Christ.
b.s: The library holds only notices and fragments (PG 5), but they show why he matters: an early canon list, a Quartodeciman Paschal theology, and one of the first Christian apologies to an emperor.

b.bio: Macarius Chrysocephalus, Metropolitan of Philadelphia, a fourteenth-century Byzantine prelate. Fabricius dates him to the fourteenth century on the grounds that a Macarius, archbishop of Philadelphia, was among the many prelates present at the synod of Constantinople in 1351 at which Barlaam and Gregory Acindynus were condemned. His surname derives from his practice of arranging extracts from the Fathers under headings he called 'golden heads' (chrysa kephalaia). Oxford manuscripts preserve dated evidence of him in 1344 (MS Barocci 156) and works copied at the end of the fifteenth century (MS Barocci 211).
b.s: The library holds one work under his name (PG 150), a canonical-disciplinary text treating marriage, widowhood, and pious practices, pronouncing lifelong rejection or anathema for cases such as marriage with two brothers, elderly widows remarrying, women adopting male dress for piety, and cutting hair as a show of godliness.

b.bio: Matthew Asen Kantakouzenos, son of Emperor John VI Kantakouzenos and Irene Asanina, received part of Thrace as an appanage in 1347 for supporting his father in the civil war against John V Palaiologos, and was proclaimed joint emperor in April 1353. From his Thracian domain he waged wars against the Serbs; an attack planned in 1350 failed when his Turkish auxiliaries defected. Captured in 1357 by his enemies, who delivered him to John V, he was compelled to abdicate in December of that year. He later served as Despot of the Morea from 1380 to 1381.
b.s: The work held here is a substantial treatise on the Church and sacraments that defends Hesychast positions against Barlaam, Gregory Akindynos, Constantine Mouzalon, and others, arguing for patriarchal authority over stavropegia and episcopal succession while expounding Christology and the Song of Songs as a hymn to Christ.

b.bio: A Greek monk, brother of Lucas Chrysoberges, active around 1400. Though Byzantine, he wrote in defense of Latin doctrine on the procession of the Holy Spirit, addressing letters to the people of Constantinople and other correspondents. His antagonist was Nilus Damyla. The Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography notes that the Quaestiones Sacrae Miscellaneae by 'Maximus the Monk' in a Vienna manuscript may or may not be his; the library's attribution rests on the De processione Spiritus Sancti printed in PG 154.
b.s: The work held here is his De processione Spiritus Sancti (PG 154, 1217–1229), a polemic defending the Filioque against Photius and those who say the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, arguing that hatred of the Latins breeds rejection of their doctrine.

b.bio: Matthaios Kamariotis was a Greek scholar from Thessaloniki who taught in Constantinople before and after the Turkish capture of 1453; when Gennadius Scholarios, his pupil, became patriarch, he appointed him instructor, and he served as first director of the re-founded Patriarchal Academy. He was influenced by Scholarios and attacked Plethon on fate. William Smith's Dictionary conflates him with Gennadius Scholarios himself (claiming he tutored Scholarios and became patriarch under the name Gennadius); that account describes a different arrangement of the same name and should not be relied on. Sources disagree on his birth date (late 14th century per Macedonian Heritage, early 15th per Springer) and death year (1489 or 1490).
b.s: The work held here is his rhetoric: a treatment of the three genres of speech (deliberative aiming at the useful, judicial at the just, panegyrical at the honorable), largely built on and argued against Hermogenes.

b.bio: No author of this name is known from other evidence. Those sources describe Pope Martin V (Oddone Colonna), elected at Constance on 11 November 1417 and died 20 February 1431, whose election effectively ended the Western Schism — a fifteenth-century pope whose writings are not patristic and do not belong in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 30. A short anonymous Latin appendix printed under this name may come from late antiquity, so the attribution to this name is uncertain.
b.s: The work held here is a brief anonymous appendix misfiled under a papal name; it has no established connection to Pope Martin V.
